lesson.intro: Internship postings regularly ask for familiarity with CI/CD and the cloud, because shipping code is part of the job, not just writing it. This pack follows code from your laptop to production: environments and secrets, builds and artifacts, a GitHub Actions workflow line by line, deployment strategies, the core cloud services on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, containers, observability, and security and cost habits. It ends with deploying a site and an API for free.
objectives: Keep configuration and secrets out of code and promote one tested artifact through dev, staging and production
Read and write a GitHub Actions workflow with triggers, jobs, steps, caching and a matrix
Choose between rolling, blue-green, canary and feature-flag releases, and plan a rollback
Map compute, storage, database, queue, CDN and DNS needs onto AWS, Azure and Google Cloud services
Use logs, metrics, traces and SLOs to run a service, and deploy a static site and an API yourself

sections.title: Environments, configuration and secrets
sections.body:
Your app works on your laptop. Before real users see it, it usually passes through several **environments**: separate copies of the app with their own servers, databases and settings.

- **Development (dev)**: your machine or a shared dev server. Fake data, debug logging, fast feedback.
- **Staging**: a copy that mirrors production as closely as you can afford (same OS, same database engine, same kind of configuration) but with its own data. It is where you catch "works on my machine" problems before customers do.
- **Production (prod)**: what users hit. Real data, real money and the strictest access.

The code should be the same everywhere. What changes is **configuration**: database addresses, API keys, feature switches, log levels. The widely followed Twelve-Factor App guidelines say to keep config in **environment variables**, not in code. Your code reads `process.env.DATABASE_URL` in Node or `os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]` in Python, and each environment sets a different value. One build then runs anywhere, and nobody edits code to deploy.

Some config values are **secrets**: database passwords, API keys, signing keys, OAuth client secrets. They need extra care:

- Never commit them. Locally, keep them in a `.env` file listed in `.gitignore`, and commit a `.env.example` with the variable names and placeholder values so teammates know what to set.
- In CI, store them as encrypted repository or environment secrets.
- In the cloud, use a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Google Secret Manager) or your platform's encrypted settings, with separate values per environment. A staging key must never unlock production.

Two habits prevent most config bugs. First, **fail fast**: check required variables at startup and refuse to start with a clear message, instead of crashing on the first request an hour later. Second, remember that environment variables are always **strings**. `DEBUG=false` gives you the string `"false"`, which is truthy in JavaScript and Python, so parse values explicitly: `process.env.DEBUG === 'true'`, `Number(process.env.PORT)`.
sections.code:
# Commit .env.example (names and placeholders). Keep the real .env out of git.
cat .env.example
# DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/shop_dev
# PAYMENT_API_KEY=replace-me
# LOG_LEVEL=debug
cp .env.example .env        # then fill in your real local values
echo ".env" >> .gitignore

# Set a variable for one command only
PORT=8080 node server.js

# Set it for the rest of this shell session, then read it
export LOG_LEVEL=info
echo "$LOG_LEVEL"
# info
sections.pitfall: Committing a `.env` file or pasting a key into code "just for now". Bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes. Add `.env` to `.gitignore` before you create the file.

activity.title: Strings, not booleans
activity.prompt: This is a startup config loader. It fails fast when a required variable is missing, which is good, but it also has a classic bug: run it and look at `debug` for an environment that set `DEBUG` to "false".

props.task: Fix the debug line so it is true only when DEBUG is the string "true". The first line should show debug: false.
props.expectOutput:
{ port: 8080, debug: false, databaseUrl: "postgres://db:5432/shop" }
Refusing to start: missing DATABASE_URL

check.question: The same Docker image runs in staging and in production. How should it find the right database in each?
choices: Build a separate image per environment with the URL written into the code
The app checks its hostname and picks a URL from a list in the code
Each environment sets DATABASE_URL, and the app reads it at startup
Keep a git branch per environment, each with its own URL
check.explanation: Configuration that differs between environments belongs in the environment, so one tested artifact runs everywhere. Per-environment images or branches mean production runs something staging never tested.

sections.title: Builds and artifacts
sections.body:
Between `git push` and a running server sits the **build**: the steps that turn source code into something a machine can run. For a JavaScript front end that means installing dependencies, then bundling and minifying (`vite build`). For Java it means compiling to bytecode and packaging a JAR. A Go service compiles to a single binary. Almost anything can also be built into a Docker image.

The output of a build is an **artifact**: a `dist/` folder of static files, a `.jar`, a Python wheel, a binary or a container image. Artifacts are what you deploy, and three rules make deployments predictable:

- **Build once, deploy many.** Build the artifact one time, test it, then promote that same artifact from staging to production. Rebuilding for production could pick up a different dependency version or compiler, so the thing you ship would not be the thing you tested. Only configuration changes between environments.
- **Version artifacts and never change them.** Tag each one with something unique, usually the git commit SHA (`shop-api:3f2a9c1`) and, for releases, a semantic version (`1.4.2`). Never overwrite a tag with different contents. Then you can always answer "what exactly is running in production?", and you can roll back by redeploying an older tag.
- **Make builds reproducible.** Commit the lock file (`package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock`, `go.sum`) and install with `npm ci` in automation. Unlike `npm install`, `npm ci` installs exactly what the lock file says, deletes any existing `node_modules` first, and fails if `package.json` and the lock file disagree. Pin base images and tool versions too.

Artifacts live in a store that matches their type: container images in a **registry** (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Azure Container Registry, Google Artifact Registry), libraries in npm or PyPI, and files such as `dist/` in object storage or as CI artifacts.

A build is also the first quality gate. If the code does not compile, a test fails or the linter finds an error, the build fails and nothing is deployed. Running that gate automatically on every push is exactly what CI does.
sections.code:
# A typical build for a Node service: the same commands CI will run
npm ci                    # exact versions from package-lock.json
npm run lint
npm test
npm run build             # writes dist/

# Name the artifact after the commit it came from
SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
echo "$SHA"
# 3f2a9c1
docker build -t ghcr.io/acme/shop-api:"$SHA" .
docker push ghcr.io/acme/shop-api:"$SHA"

# Later, promote the SAME image to production by its tag. Never rebuild it.
sections.tip: If someone asks which version is in production, the answer should be one commit SHA you can look up in git.
sections.pitfall: Running `npm install` in CI. It can rewrite the lock file and resolve different versions from the ones you tested. Use `npm ci`, which installs exactly what the lock file pins and fails loudly if it is out of date.

check.question: Why deploy the exact artifact that passed staging instead of rebuilding the same commit for production?
choices: A rebuild can pull in different dependency or tool versions, so production would run something never tested
Git does not allow the same commit to be built twice
Production servers are not allowed to run builds
Artifacts expire after their first deployment
check.explanation: Builds depend on more than the commit: registries, base images and tools change. Promoting one immutable artifact guarantees that what passed staging is byte for byte what reaches production.

sections.title: CI with GitHub Actions, line by line
sections.body:
**Continuous integration (CI)** means every push and pull request is built and tested automatically, so problems show up within minutes instead of at release time. GitHub Actions is the CI system built into GitHub and the one you are most likely to meet first; GitLab CI, CircleCI and Jenkins use the same ideas with different syntax.

A **workflow** is a YAML file in `.github/workflows/`. Walk through the one below:

- `name: CI` is the label shown in the Actions tab and on pull requests.
- `on:` lists the **triggers**. This workflow runs on pushes to `main` and on every pull request. Other common triggers are `workflow_dispatch` (a manual Run button) and `schedule` with a cron expression.
- `jobs:` holds one or more **jobs**. Jobs run **in parallel** by default, each on a fresh virtual machine called a **runner**; `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` picks a GitHub-hosted Linux runner. To make one job wait for another, give it `needs: test`.
- `strategy.matrix` runs the job once per combination of values. `node-version: [22, 24]` creates two jobs, and the steps read the current value as `${{ matrix.node-version }}`. Two lists with 2 and 3 values would create 6 jobs.
- `steps:` run in order inside a job, and the job stops at the first step that fails. A step either **uses** a reusable action or **runs** shell commands. `uses: actions/checkout@v6` clones your repository into the runner, which starts empty. `run: npm test` runs a command. `with:` passes inputs to an action.
- `cache: npm` tells `actions/setup-node` to save npm's download cache, keyed by a hash of `package-lock.json`, and restore it on later runs. Packages then come from the cache instead of the network until the lock file changes.

When the run finishes, GitHub shows a green check or a red X on the commit and the pull request. Make the job a **required status check** in the branch protection rules, and nobody can merge a red pull request.

Secrets such as deploy tokens go in the repository settings and are read as `${{ secrets.NAME }}`. GitHub masks them in logs and does not pass them to workflows triggered by pull requests from forks. Keep CI fast with caching and by splitting slow suites: a pipeline that takes 40 minutes is one that people start to skip.
sections.code:
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [22, 24]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
sections.pitfall: Forgetting `actions/checkout`. The runner starts with an empty workspace, so `npm ci` fails because there is no package.json. Checkout is almost always the first step.

check.question: In the workflow above, what does `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` give each job?
choices: The same Linux version your users run
A long-lived server that keeps files from earlier runs
The newest runner that already has your dependencies installed
A fresh GitHub-hosted Linux virtual machine
check.explanation: Each job gets a clean, GitHub-hosted runner that is thrown away afterwards. That is why every job checks out the code and installs dependencies, and why caching exists.

sections.title: Continuous delivery and deployment strategies
sections.body:
CI proves a commit is good. **CD** gets it to users, and the term covers two levels:

- **Continuous delivery**: every commit that passes the pipeline is ready to release, and deploying to production is one button press, often behind a manual approval.
- **Continuous deployment**: every commit that passes goes to production automatically, with no human step.

A typical pipeline: build and test, deploy the artifact to staging, run smoke tests against it, wait for approval if required, deploy the same artifact to production, then watch the dashboards. In GitHub Actions, a deploy job uses `needs:` to wait for the tests, `if:` to run only on `main`, and an `environment:` whose protection rules can require a reviewer.

How you replace the old version matters as much as when:

- **Recreate**: stop the old version, then start the new one. Simple, but users see downtime.
- **Rolling**: replace instances a few at a time behind the load balancer. No downtime and no extra servers, but for a while both versions serve traffic, and rolling back means rolling again.
- **Blue-green**: run the new version (green) next to the old one (blue) at full size, test it, then switch the router to green. Rollback is switching back, which takes seconds. The cost is two full environments during the switch.
- **Canary**: send a small share of real traffic, say 5 percent, to the new version, compare its error rate and latency with the old one, and raise the share step by step. A bad release hurts few users and can be rolled back automatically.
- **Feature flags**: ship code switched off and turn it on in configuration, for internal users first, then for a percentage of everyone. This separates **deploy** (the code is on the servers) from **release** (users see it), and a flag doubles as an instant kill switch. Delete old flags, or they pile up as dead code paths.

Whatever the strategy, plan the **rollback** before you deploy: usually, redeploy the previous artifact tag. Database changes are the hard part, because data does not roll back. Use **expand and contract**: first add new columns or tables in a backward-compatible way, deploy code that works with both shapes, and remove the old shape only in a later release.
sections.code:
# Added under jobs: in the CI workflow from the previous section
jobs:
  # test: ...as before

  deploy-staging:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh staging "${{ github.sha }}"
      - run: ./scripts/smoke-test.sh https://staging.example.com

  deploy-production:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production # protection rule: a reviewer must approve
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh production "${{ github.sha }}"
sections.pitfall: Shipping a change that is not backward compatible, such as renaming a database column the old version still reads. During a rolling or canary deploy both versions run at once, so every change must work with both.

activity.title: Roll out a feature flag
activity.prompt: Percentage rollouts hash each user id into a stable bucket from 0 to 99, so the same user always gets the same answer as the percentage grows. Run it at 10 percent and note who sees the new checkout.

props.task: Raise the rollout to 50 percent. Predict who switches before you run it: only users whose bucket is below 50 change, and nobody who already had NEW loses it.
props.expectOutput:
dev-ana bucket 51 NEW
u-1001 bucket 1 NEW
u-1002 bucket 44 NEW
u-1003 bucket 63 old
u-1004 bucket 58 old
u-1005 bucket 77 old
u-1006 bucket 20 NEW

check.question: You want 5 percent of real users on the new version while you compare its error rate with the old one, then raise the share step by step. Which strategy is that?
choices: Blue-green
Canary
Recreate
Rolling
check.explanation: A canary sends a small, growing share of traffic to the new version while you compare metrics. Blue-green switches all traffic at once, and a rolling deploy replaces instances without comparing the two versions on purpose.

sections.title: Cloud basics: regions, service models and core services
sections.body:
"The cloud" means renting computers, storage and managed software by the second or by the request instead of buying servers. The big three providers are **AWS** (Amazon), **Azure** (Microsoft) and **Google Cloud**. Their consoles look different, but they sell the same building blocks, and job postings often name one. Learn the categories and you can map any provider's names onto them.

Infrastructure is split into **regions** (a geographic area such as us-east-1 or West Europe), and most regions contain several **availability zones**: separate data centers with independent power and networking. Run at least two instances in different zones, and one data center failure does not take you down. Pick regions close to your users for lower latency, and in the jurisdiction where your data must stay.

Services differ in how much the provider manages for you:

- **IaaS** (infrastructure as a service): you rent virtual machines and manage the OS, patches, runtime and app. Most control, most work.
- **PaaS** (platform as a service): you push code or a container, and the platform runs, scales and patches it. Examples are Heroku, Render, Google App Engine, Azure App Service and AWS Elastic Beanstalk.
- **SaaS** (software as a service): finished software you simply use, such as Gmail, Slack or GitHub.
- **Serverless functions**: you upload a function that runs per request, scales to zero and bills per invocation. The trade-offs are **cold starts** (a delay while a new instance starts), execution time limits and less control over the runtime.

Under every model the **shared responsibility model** applies: the provider secures the hardware and data centers, and you secure what you put on them, including your code, data, access rules and configuration. Most cloud breaches start on the customer's side, such as a storage bucket accidentally left public.

The table lists the core services with each provider's name. **Object storage** deserves a special mention: it stores files (objects) by key inside buckets, cheaply and durably, and it is where uploads, backups, logs and static sites go. A **CDN** caches content at edge locations near users, **queues** let one service hand work to another without waiting, and **DNS** points your domain at all of it.
sections.code:
What you need          AWS                Azure                      Google Cloud
Virtual machines       EC2                Virtual Machines           Compute Engine

Run containers         ECS with Fargate   Container Apps             Cloud Run

sections.pitfall: Running production on one instance in one availability zone. A single server or data center failure then takes the whole app down. Spread instances across at least two zones.

check.question: On an IaaS virtual machine such as EC2, who installs operating system security patches?
choices: You, the customer
The cloud provider, automatically
Nobody, because a running VM cannot be patched
The provider, but only for Windows machines
check.explanation: With IaaS the provider runs the hardware and the virtualization layer, and everything from the OS up is yours. Moving to PaaS or serverless is how you hand OS patching to the provider.

sections.title: Containers in production
sections.body:
Docker Basics showed how to build and run a container on your own machine. In production the same image runs on servers you may never log into, so the workflow becomes:

- CI builds the image and tags it with the commit SHA.
- CI pushes it to a **registry**, such as Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`), Amazon ECR, Azure Container Registry or Google Artifact Registry. Production pulls from there.
- A deploy tells the platform which tag to run. Avoid deploying `:latest`: it is a moving label, so you cannot tell which code is running, two servers can pull different images, and a rollback has no fixed tag to return to.

Running one container is easy. Running dozens across many machines, restarting the ones that crash, spreading them across zones, rolling out new versions and sending traffic only to healthy ones is **orchestration**. **Kubernetes** is the standard orchestrator, and every big cloud offers it as a managed service (EKS, AKS, GKE). Its core ideas are worth knowing even if you never write the YAML yourself:

- A **cluster** is a set of machines called **nodes**, run by a control plane.
- A **Pod** is the smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that share a network address.
- A **Deployment** declares the desired state, such as "3 replicas of shop-api:3f2a9c1". Controllers keep comparing reality with that declaration and fix differences, replacing crashed Pods and performing a rolling update when you change the tag.
- A **Service** gives a changing set of Pods one stable name and address, and load-balances across them.
- **Probes** check health. When a **readiness** probe fails, the Pod is taken out of the Service until it recovers. When a **liveness** probe fails, the container is restarted.
- **ConfigMaps** and **Secrets** inject configuration as environment variables or files.

Kubernetes is powerful but a lot to operate. For a small team, a managed container platform such as Google Cloud Run, AWS ECS with Fargate or Azure Container Apps runs your image with autoscaling and HTTPS and no cluster to manage.

Whatever runs them, production containers should be **stateless**: keep data in a managed database or object storage, not on the container's file system, which disappears when the container is replaced. Write logs to standard output and let the platform collect them.
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: shop-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: shop-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: shop-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/shop-api:3f2a9c1 # a commit tag, never latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: DATABASE_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: shop-secrets
                  key: database-url
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: shop-api
spec:
  selector:
    app: shop-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
sections.pitfall: Saving uploaded files or sessions on the container's disk. The next deploy or restart replaces the container and the data is gone, and the other replicas never see it. Put files in object storage and sessions in a database or cache.

check.question: A Pod's readiness probe starts failing while its liveness probe still passes. What does Kubernetes do?
choices: Restarts the container immediately
Deletes the Deployment
Stops sending it traffic through the Service until the readiness probe passes again
Scales the Deployment down to zero replicas
check.explanation: Readiness answers "can this Pod take traffic right now?", so failing it only removes the Pod from load balancing. Restarts are triggered by the liveness probe.

sections.title: Observability and on-call
sections.body:
Once code is in production, you need to answer "is it working, and if not, why?" without attaching a debugger. That is **observability**, and it rests on three kinds of signals:

- **Logs**: timestamped records of events. Write them as **structured** JSON with fields such as level, message, request id and version, so you can search and filter ("all errors for request req_8f2c41"). Never log passwords, tokens or card numbers.
- **Metrics**: numbers aggregated over time, cheap to store and fast to graph: requests per second, error rate, latency, queue depth, CPU. For a service, start with **RED**: Rate, Errors, Duration.
- **Traces**: the path of one request through several services, as a tree of timed **spans**. A trace shows that a slow checkout spent 1.8 seconds waiting on the payments service. **OpenTelemetry** is the vendor-neutral standard for producing all three signals.

Look at latency as **percentiles**, not averages. p50 is the median; p99 is the time that 99 percent of requests beat, the experience of your slowest 1 percent, which at scale is a lot of people. An average of 120 ms can hide a p99 of 3 seconds.

Turn the signals into goals:

- An **SLI** (service level indicator) is a measurement, such as the share of requests that succeed in under 300 ms.
- An **SLO** (objective) is the target for it, such as 99.9 percent over 30 days.
- An **SLA** (agreement) is a contract with customers, with penalties, usually set looser than the SLO.
- The **error budget** is what the SLO allows to fail: 0.1 percent of 30 days is 43.2 minutes. While budget remains, ship features; when it runs out, prioritize reliability.

**Alerts** should page a human only for symptoms users feel, such as a high error rate or an error budget burning fast, and every page should need action. Causes such as high CPU belong on dashboards or in tickets; paging on them teaches people to ignore pages.

**On-call** means taking turns being the person who responds. During an incident, **mitigate first** (roll back, switch off the flag, add capacity), then find the root cause. Afterwards, write a **blameless postmortem**: what happened, the timeline, why the system allowed it, and follow-up actions, without blaming individuals. **Runbooks**, short documents saying what to check for each alert, make a 3 a.m. page far less painful.
sections.pitfall: Paging on causes such as CPU above 80 percent. CPU can be high while users are fine, and users can suffer while CPU is low. Page on user-facing symptoms and send the rest to dashboards.

activity.title: Averages hide the tail
activity.prompt: Run this on 20 real-looking checkout latencies. Compare the average with p50 and p95, then compute an error budget.

props.task: Replace the TODO so fourNines is the error budget for a 99.99% SLO over 30 days. Predict it first: one more nine divides the budget by ten.
props.expectOutput:
average: 389 ms
p50: 99 ms
p95: 2900 ms
99.9% over 30 days: 43.2 minutes
99.99% over 30 days: 4.3 minutes

check.question: Your service's average latency is 120 ms, but its p99 is 3 seconds. What does that tell you?
choices: The service is healthy, because the average is low
99 percent of requests take about 3 seconds
The metrics must be wrong, because p99 cannot be that far above the average
About 1 request in 100 takes 3 seconds or more, which the average hides
check.explanation: p99 is the latency that 99 percent of requests stay under, so the slowest 1 percent take at least 3 seconds. A few very slow requests barely move an average, which is why percentiles are the standard.

sections.title: Security and cost hygiene
sections.body:
Two of the fastest ways to make the news, or to get an alarming bill, are leaked credentials and forgotten resources. A few habits prevent most of it.

**Least privilege.** Every person, service and pipeline gets only the permissions it needs, on only the resources it needs. A service that reads product images gets read access to one bucket, not `s3:*` on everything. Services should assume **roles** instead of using personal keys. Never use the root or owner account for daily work, turn on multi-factor authentication for every human, and remove permissions that nothing uses.

**Short-lived credentials.** Long-lived access keys get copied into laptops, scripts and CI settings, and they leak from there. Prefer credentials that expire in minutes. In CI, GitHub Actions can use **OpenID Connect (OIDC)**: the workflow proves its identity to AWS, Azure or Google Cloud and receives a temporary token for one role, so no cloud key is stored in GitHub at all. The workflow below deploys a site that way.

**Never commit secrets.** If one does get pushed:

- **Revoke or rotate it immediately.** Assume it is already stolen: automated scanners harvest keys from public repositories within minutes.
- Then remove it from the code, and rewrite history if needed. Deleting the line in a new commit is not enough, because the old commit still contains it, and so do forks and clones.
- Check the provider's logs for anything the key was used for.

GitHub secret scanning and push protection catch many known key formats, and tools like gitleaks run the same check locally or in CI. Keep dependencies patched too: Dependabot or Renovate opens pull requests for vulnerable packages.

**Cost hygiene.** Cloud bills grow quietly. Set a **budget alert** on day one. **Tag** resources with an owner and a project, so every charge has a name next to it. Shut down or delete what you are not using: a forgotten GPU instance or managed database can cost more than everything else combined. Watch **data transfer out** of the cloud (egress), which is billed per gigabyte, and always-on extras such as NAT gateways and load balancers. Use autoscaling and serverless options that scale to zero for small or spiky workloads. Free tiers are generous for learning, but they have limits, and many require a card on file, so a leaked key can still run up a real bill.
sections.code:
# Deploy a built site to S3 with short-lived AWS credentials: no stored keys
name: Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write # lets the job request an OIDC token from GitHub
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci && npm run build
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/shop-site-deploy
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: aws s3 sync dist/ s3://shop-site --delete
sections.pitfall: Deleting a leaked key from the code in a new commit and moving on. The key is still in git history and has probably been copied already. Revoke it first, then clean up.

activity.title: Read a least-privilege policy
activity.prompt: This AWS IAM policy belongs to the shop's image service. Before the quiz, work out exactly what it can do: which actions, on which buckets and paths. Notice everything it cannot do, such as deleting objects or touching any other bucket.

check.question: A developer pushed an AWS access key to a public GitHub repository ten minutes ago. What should happen first?
choices: Push a commit that deletes the key from the file
Deactivate the key in AWS and issue a new one
Make the repository private
Rewrite git history and force push
check.explanation: Scanners may already have copied the key, so the only safe first move is making it useless. Cleaning the repository and history comes after, because the key is compromised either way.

sections.title: Hands-on: deploy a static site and a small API for free
sections.body:
Time to ship something. This walkthrough puts a static front end (such as a Vite React app) and a small Node API online without paying, using free tiers that exist at the time of writing. Free plans change, so check each provider's current limits.

**Part 1: the static site.** A Vite build is just files, so any static host works: Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages or GitHub Pages.

- Push the project to GitHub, and check that `npm run build` works locally and writes `dist/`.
- Sign in to the host with GitHub and import the repository.
- Set the build command to `npm run build` and the publish (output) directory to `dist`. Add `VITE_` variables, such as `VITE_API_URL`, in the host's environment settings.
- Deploy. You get an HTTPS URL, every push to `main` redeploys, and most hosts build a **preview URL** for each pull request, which is great for code review.
- With client-side routing, add a rewrite to `index.html` (on Netlify, a `public/_redirects` file containing `/* /index.html 200`).

To keep everything inside GitHub instead, the workflow below deploys to GitHub Pages with Actions. Set the Pages source to GitHub Actions in the repository settings, and for a project site set `base: '/repo-name/'` in `vite.config.js`, because the site is served from a subpath.

**Part 2: the API.** An API needs a running process, so use a PaaS free tier such as Render, or a container service such as Google Cloud Run.

- Read the port from the environment: `const port = process.env.PORT || 3000`. Platforms choose the port and route traffic to it.
- Add a `GET /health` endpoint that returns 200, and point the platform's health check at it.
- On Render, create a Web Service from the repository, set the build command (`npm ci`) and start command (`node server.js`), and add environment variables in the dashboard. Free instances sleep after 15 minutes without traffic and take about a minute to wake, which is fine for a portfolio project.
- On Cloud Run, from the project folder: `gcloud run deploy shop-api --source . --region us-central1 --allow-unauthenticated`.
- Allow your site's origin in the API's **CORS** settings, or the browser will block the front end's requests.

**Part 3: check and connect.** Smoke-test with `curl -i https://api.example.com/health`, then set `VITE_API_URL` on the static host and redeploy. Optionally add a custom domain: create the DNS record the host shows you (usually a CNAME), and HTTPS certificates are issued automatically. Put both URLs in your README and on your resume. A live project with CI behind it is exactly what internship reviewers like to click.
sections.code:
name: Deploy site

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v4
        with:
          path: dist

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
sections.tip: Add a CI badge and the live URL to the top of your README. Reviewers spend seconds on a repository, and both show at a glance that the project builds and runs.

check.question: Your site at https://shop.example.com calls your API at https://api.example.com, and the browser console shows a CORS error. Where does the fix go?
choices: In the API: allow the site's origin in its CORS response headers
In the site: add mode: 'no-cors' and read the JSON as usual
In DNS: point both names at the same IP address
In each user's browser: turn off web security
check.explanation: The browser blocks the response unless the API says the site's origin is allowed, through headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin. no-cors mode only returns an opaque response whose body you cannot read.

keyTerms.definition: A separate running copy of an app, such as dev, staging or production, with its own data and config.
A named string set outside the code that tells the app how to behave in that environment.
A credential such as a password or API key that must never be committed or logged.
The versioned, deployable output of a build: static files, a JAR, a binary or an image.
Building and testing every push and pull request automatically.
Keeping every passing commit releasable, with production deploys triggered by a person.
Sending a small, growing share of traffic to a new version while comparing its metrics.
A config switch that turns code on for some or all users without a redeploy.
An isolated data center within a cloud region, with its own power and networking.
A server that stores and serves container images, such as ghcr.io or Amazon ECR.
A reliability target for a measured indicator, such as 99.9 percent of requests succeeding over 30 days.
Granting each identity only the permissions it needs, on only the resources it needs.

summary: Same code everywhere, different config: environment variables per environment, secrets in a secret manager, never in git.
Build once, tag the artifact with the commit SHA, and promote that exact artifact; npm ci keeps builds reproducible.
A GitHub Actions workflow is triggers plus parallel jobs on fresh runners, each running ordered steps; checkout comes first and caching keeps it fast.
Rolling, blue-green, canary and feature flags trade cost, speed and risk; always plan the rollback and keep migrations backward compatible.
The clouds sell the same building blocks under different names; run across zones, keep containers stateless and know who patches what.
Watch percentiles and SLOs, page only on user-facing symptoms, use least privilege with short-lived credentials, and set a budget alert on day one.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who just finished a coding bootcamp what happens between git push and users seeing their change: what CI checks, what an artifact is, how a canary or blue-green release limits the damage of a bad deploy, and how they would know in production that something broke.

questions.question: Which of these belongs in an environment variable rather than in the code?
choices: The function that calculates sales tax
The database connection string, which differs between staging and production
The list of routes the API serves
The HTML template for the home page
questions.explanation: Values that differ between dev, staging and production, like connection strings, are configuration. Business logic, routes and templates are the same everywhere, so they stay in the code.

questions.question: Type the command that runs `node server.js` with the environment variable `PORT` set to 8080 for that one command only.
questions.explanation: Prefixing NAME=value sets the variable only in the environment of that command. export would set it for the rest of the shell session.

questions.question: Production was started with `DEBUG=false`, yet it logs request bodies. Why?
choices: process.env is only read in development builds
DEBUG is a reserved name that is always true
console.log ignores environment variables
Environment variables are strings, and the non-empty string "false" is truthy
questions.explanation: process.env values are always strings, and any non-empty string is truthy, including "false". Compare explicitly: process.env.DEBUG === 'true'.

questions.question: Type the npm command that installs exactly the versions in package-lock.json and fails if package.json and the lock file disagree.
questions.explanation: npm ci (clean install) removes node_modules and installs exactly what the lock file pins, which makes CI builds reproducible. npm install may update the lock file instead.

questions.question: Type the git command that prints the short SHA of the current commit, for tagging an artifact.
questions.explanation: rev-parse turns a name such as HEAD into a commit id, and --short abbreviates it, usually to 7 characters. The same SHA then links the image back to its exact source.

questions.question: Match each project to the artifact its build produces.

pairs.right: A dist/ folder of static files
A JAR file
A wheel (.whl) published to PyPI
An image pushed to a registry
A single compiled binary

questions.explanation: Every build ends in something deployable: static files, a JAR, a wheel, an image or a binary. Whatever the type, version it and never change it after it is built.

questions.question: Production runs `shop-api:3f2a9c1`. The new release `shop-api:8d41e07` causes errors. What is the fastest safe rollback?
choices: Revert the commit, then wait for CI to build a fresh image
SSH into each server and edit the code by hand
Redeploy the shop-api:3f2a9c1 image that ran before
Rebuild 3f2a9c1 from source on the production servers
questions.explanation: The previous image is immutable, already tested and still in the registry, so redeploying its tag restores the known good version in minutes. Reverting and rebuilding works too, but it is slower and produces a new, untested artifact.

questions.question: Where must GitHub Actions workflow files live?
choices: In .github/workflows/ in the repository
In .github/actions.yml at the root
In workflows/ at the repository root
In .ci/ in the repository
questions.explanation: GitHub looks for workflow YAML files in the .github/workflows directory of the repository. Files anywhere else are ignored.

questions.question: Fill the blank so the workflow also runs for every pull request.
choices: pull-request
pr
pull_request
merge_request
questions.explanation: The event name is pull_request, with an underscore. By default it fires when a pull request is opened, reopened or gets new commits.

questions.question: A job's matrix has `node-version: [22, 24]` and `os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]`. How many jobs does it start?
questions.explanation: A matrix runs every combination: 2 Node versions times 2 operating systems is 4 jobs, which run in parallel.

questions.question: In this job, `npm ci` fails with an error saying it cannot find package.json. What is missing?
questions.code:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
choices: A cache: npm input on setup-node
A uses: actions/checkout@v6 step before setup-node
A needs: build line on the job
Quotes around the Node version
questions.explanation: A runner starts with an empty workspace. Without actions/checkout, the repository's files never arrive, so there is no package.json to install from.

questions.question: A workflow has `test` and `deploy` jobs. Without extra configuration, deploy starts at the same time as test. How do you make deploy wait until test passes?
choices: Put the deploy job after the test job in the file
Put both jobs in one matrix
Add if: success() to the test job
Add needs: test to the deploy job
questions.explanation: Jobs run in parallel unless needs says otherwise. With needs: test, deploy starts only after test succeeds, and is skipped if test fails. Order in the file does not matter.

questions.question: What does `cache: npm` on actions/setup-node save between runs?
choices: npm's download cache, keyed by a hash of package-lock.json
The node_modules folder, keyed by the branch name
The built dist/ folder, so the build step can be skipped
Test results, so passing tests do not run again
questions.explanation: setup-node caches npm's global download cache and keys it on a hash of the lock file. npm ci still runs, but it installs from the cache instead of downloading every package again.

questions.question: Put the life of a pull request's CI run in order.
items: You push a commit to the pull request's branch
GitHub triggers the workflow's pull_request event
A fresh runner starts and checks out the code
Steps install dependencies, lint and run the tests
The result appears as a status check on the pull request
The pull request can merge once the required checks pass
questions.explanation: Each push triggers the workflow, a fresh runner checks out the code and runs the steps, and the result becomes a status check. Branch protection uses required checks to decide whether merging is allowed.

questions.question: Match each deployment strategy to how it works.

pairs.right: Replace instances a few at a time
Switch all traffic between two full environments
Send a small share of traffic to the new version first
Ship code switched off, then enable it in config
Stop the old version, then start the new one

questions.explanation: Recreate accepts downtime, rolling replaces instances gradually, blue-green flips all traffic between two environments, canary tests on a slice of traffic, and feature flags separate deploying code from releasing it.

questions.question: Your pipeline deploys every commit on main to production automatically once the tests pass, with no approval step. What is this called?
choices: Continuous delivery
Continuous deployment
Continuous integration only
Blue-green deployment
questions.explanation: Continuous deployment removes the human step entirely. Continuous delivery keeps every commit releasable but leaves the production deploy to a person.

questions.question: Which strategy gives the fastest rollback, at the cost of running two full copies of production for a while?
choices: Rolling
Recreate
Blue-green
Canary at 1 percent
questions.explanation: In blue-green the old environment keeps running, so rolling back is a router switch. A rolling deploy has to roll back instance by instance, and recreate needs a full redeploy.

questions.question: Why must database migrations stay backward compatible during a rolling or canary deploy, and what is the expand and contract pattern?
questions.answer: During the rollout the old and new versions run at the same time against the same database, so a change the old code cannot handle breaks it. Expand and contract first adds the new shape next to the old one, deploys code that works with both, and removes the old shape only in a later release.
questions.explanation: Code can be rolled back in seconds, but data and schema changes cannot, so schema changes are split across releases.

questions.question: Match each AWS service to what it does.

pairs.right: Virtual machines
Object storage
Managed relational database
Message queue
CDN
DNS

questions.explanation: These six cover most small applications: compute, file storage, a relational database, a queue, a CDN and DNS. Azure and Google Cloud sell the same categories under other names.

questions.question: Match each Azure or Google Cloud service to its AWS equivalent.

pairs.right: Amazon S3
Amazon EC2
AWS Lambda
Amazon RDS
Amazon EKS

questions.explanation: The big three offer the same building blocks: Blob Storage and S3 are object storage, Compute Engine and EC2 are VMs, Azure Functions and Lambda are serverless functions, Cloud SQL and RDS are managed SQL, and AKS and EKS are managed Kubernetes.

questions.question: You deploy by pushing code, and the platform handles servers, OS patches and scaling, but you still own the app and its data. Which service model is that?
choices: PaaS
IaaS
SaaS
On-premises hosting
questions.explanation: PaaS runs your code on a managed platform. With IaaS you would manage the OS yourself, and with SaaS you would not write the app at all.

questions.question: Why run instances in at least two availability zones?
choices: So users in other countries get lower latency
Because each zone allows only one instance
To avoid paying for data transfer
So the app survives the failure of one data center in the region
questions.explanation: Zones are separate data centers within a region, with independent power and networking. Spreading instances across them keeps the app up when one zone fails. Latency for distant users is a question of regions, not zones.

questions.question: Which statements about serverless functions such as AWS Lambda are true? Select all that apply.
choices: You pay per invocation and execution time
They can scale to zero when there is no traffic
A new instance can add cold start latency
They suit jobs that run for many hours
You patch the operating system they run on
questions.explanation: Functions bill per invocation and run time, scale to zero and can add cold start latency. They have execution time limits (15 minutes on Lambda), so multi-hour jobs do not fit, and the provider patches the OS for you.

questions.question: Type the command that uploads the local image `ghcr.io/acme/shop-api:3f2a9c1` to its registry.
questions.explanation: docker push sends the image's layers to the registry named at the start of the image name, here GitHub Container Registry. You must be logged in to it first with docker login.

questions.question: Why is deploying `shop-api:latest` to production a bad idea?
choices: Registries delete images tagged latest after a day
latest moves with every push, so you cannot tell what is running and have no fixed tag to roll back to
Kubernetes refuses to run images tagged latest
Images tagged latest are built without their dependencies
questions.explanation: latest is just a tag that moves whenever someone pushes. Commit-SHA tags never change, so they tell you exactly what is running and give rollbacks a fixed target.

questions.question: Match each Kubernetes term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers
Declares how many replicas of which image should run
Stable name and load balancing for a set of Pods
A machine in the cluster that runs Pods
Restarts a container that stops responding

questions.explanation: Nodes run Pods; a Deployment declares how many Pods of which image to keep running; a Service gives them one address; probes decide whether to restart a container or send it traffic.

questions.question: Users upload profile photos to your API, which runs as three container replicas. Where should the photos go?
choices: Object storage such as S3, with the database storing each photo's key
The container's /uploads folder
A volume on whichever replica handled the upload
Inside the container image, rebuilt every night
questions.explanation: Container file systems vanish on replacement and are not shared between replicas. Object storage is durable and shared, and the database only needs each photo's key.

questions.question: An availability SLO is 99.9 percent over 30 days. How many minutes of downtime does the error budget allow?
questions.explanation: The budget is 0.1 percent of 30 days: 0.001 x 30 x 24 x 60 = 43.2 minutes. At 99.99 percent it shrinks to about 4.3 minutes.

questions.question: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Timestamped records of individual events
Numbers aggregated over time, such as error rate
One request's path across services as timed spans
A target, such as 99.9 percent of requests succeeding
A contract with customers that carries penalties

questions.explanation: Logs, metrics and traces are the three signals; an SLO is your internal target and an SLA is the external promise with consequences, usually set looser than the SLO.

questions.question: Which alert is most worth waking someone up for at 3 a.m.?
choices: CPU on one server has been above 80 percent for 10 minutes
Disk usage on a log server reached 60 percent
Checkout's error rate is burning the monthly error budget fast
A dependency published a new minor version
questions.explanation: Burning the error budget fast means users are failing right now, and someone must act. High CPU, disk at 60 percent and new library versions may matter, but they belong on dashboards or in tickets.

questions.question: Put these incident response steps in order.
items: An alert fires and the on-call engineer acknowledges it
Assess the impact and tell stakeholders an incident is open
Mitigate, for example by rolling back the last deploy
Confirm that the metrics have recovered
Write a blameless postmortem with follow-up actions
questions.explanation: Acknowledge, communicate and mitigate first, so users stop hurting. Root cause analysis and the blameless postmortem come after the service is stable.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of letting GitHub Actions deploy to your cloud account through OIDC?
choices: Deployments run faster
The build artifacts are encrypted
Anyone with a fork can deploy to production
The workflow gets short-lived credentials for one role, so no long-lived cloud key is stored in GitHub
questions.explanation: With OIDC the workflow exchanges a GitHub-signed identity token for temporary credentials for one role. There is no long-lived key to leak from repository settings, and the role's trust policy can limit which repository and branch may use it.

questions.question: Which practices follow the principle of least privilege? Select all that apply.
choices: Give an image-resizing service read access to one bucket only
Use a separate CI role that can only deploy
Remove permissions a role has not used in months
Share one admin access key across the team to keep things simple
Grant s3:* on all buckets so the service never hits a permission error
questions.explanation: Least privilege means narrow, purpose-specific permissions that are reviewed over time. A shared admin key and blanket s3:* access are the opposite: one leak exposes everything.

questions.question: The repository is public. A teammate says the leak is fixed because of commit 9c2e1f0. What is wrong with that?
questions.code:
$ git log --oneline -2
9c2e1f0 Remove payment API key from config.js
4b7a3d2 Add payment integration (config.js holds the live key)
choices: The key is still in commit 4b7a3d2 and was likely harvested; it must be revoked and rotated
Commit messages must not mention API keys
The key is safe because 9c2e1f0 is the newest commit
git log shows only local commits, so the key never reached GitHub
questions.explanation: Commit 4b7a3d2 still contains the key and anyone can check it out, and scanners probably copied it within minutes of the push. Revoke and rotate the key, then clean history if needed.

questions.question: Put the steps for deploying a Vite site to a static host in order.
items: Check that npm run build writes dist/ locally
Import the repository in the host's dashboard
Set the build command to npm run build and the publish directory to dist
Deploy and open the HTTPS URL
questions.explanation: Prove the build works locally, get the code on GitHub, connect the host, tell it how to build and what to publish, then deploy. After that, every push to main redeploys.

questions.question: Type a curl command that requests https://api.example.com/health and also prints the response status line and headers.
questions.explanation: curl -i (include) prints the status line and headers before the body, so you can see the 200 and check headers such as Content-Type. Use -I to fetch headers only, which sends a HEAD request instead.

questions.question: Why should a small API read its port with `process.env.PORT || 3000` instead of always listening on 3000?
choices: Browsers block requests to port 3000
Hosting platforms assign the port through PORT and route traffic only to that port
Node can only listen on ports set by environment variables
It makes the API respond faster
questions.explanation: Platforms such as Render and Cloud Run choose the port and pass it in PORT, then route traffic only to it. The fallback keeps local development working.
